notes: 1.e4 — open the king's pawn, free the bishop and queen, plant a flag in the centre. The most popular move on the planet, and for good reason.
1...e5 — Black says 'you want the centre? so do I.' Classical and symmetrical… for now.
2.Nf3 — develop and poke the e5-pawn. Development WITH a threat is the dream.
2...Nc6 — defends e5 and develops. Textbook.
3.Bc4 — the Italian bishop, sniping at f7 — the only square the enemy king guards all by himself.
3...Bc5 — Black copies you and aims at YOUR f2. A bishop staring contest.
4.c3 — looks shy, hits hard: it's prepping d4 to build a giant centre.
4...Nf6 — develops and jabs at e4. Black pokes back.
5.d4 — boom. The big break. White grabs the centre and opens lines.
5...exd4 — Black takes; letting dxe5 happen would just be sad.
6.cxd4 — recapture, and now the dream pawns on d4+e4 are up. A textbook centre.
6...Bb4+ — a cheeky check to develop with tempo before White gets comfy.
7.Nc3 — block the check by developing. Two jobs, one knight.
7...Nxe4!? — the critical grab. Black snatches e4 and dares you to prove the gambit. Theory gets spicy here.
8.O-O — castle, king safe, rooks connected. Never attack with your king stuck in the middle.
8...Bxc3 — Black trades the pinned knight before it makes trouble.
9.d5! — the key move. Kick the c6-knight and rip open lines. You're playing for the attack, not the pawn.
9...Bf6 — the bishop retreats somewhere safe and useful instead of getting trapped.
10.Re1 — slam the rook on the e-file, right at that loose e4-knight. Pressure, pressure.
10...Ne7 — the knight scurries back to defend; Black untangles carefully.
11.Rxe4 — win the knight back; the dust settles into a rich position with your pieces buzzing.
11...d6 — Black solidifies and gives the c8-bishop a window.
12.Bg5 — develop the last bishop with a pin on e7. Annoying for Black.
12...Bxg5 — Black trades off the pinning bishop to ease the pressure.
13.Nxg5 — recapture, and the knight lands on g5 eyeing f7 and h7. Sneaky.
13...O-O — Black finally castles into safety.

14.Nxh7! — a little tactical bonus: the knight grabs h7. White emerges with an extra pawn and a pleasant, active position. The d5-pawn and active rooks give you a comfortable pull into the middlegame.
v.plan: You came out of the opening a clean pawn up with a strong protected passed pawn on d5 and active pieces. From here: keep your pieces active, especially the rook on e4 and knight, support the d5-pawn, and aim to trade down into a winning endgame where that extra pawn tells. Don't rush — your structure is better, so simplify when you can and let the d-pawn become a monster. If Black tries counterplay, just keep your king safe and convert calmly.

notes: 1.e4 — centre, freedom. You know the drill.
1...e5 — the classical reply.
2.Nf3 — develop, attack e5.
2...Nc6 — defend, develop.
3.Bc4 — bishop eyes f7, the Italian signature.
3...Bc5 — mirror match, both bishops loaded.
4.d3 — the 'Pianissimo' (very quiet) move. No fireworks — just a rock-solid build-up. This is what the world's best actually play today.
4...Nf6 — develop and eye e4. Calm and classical.
5.O-O — king to safety first. Patience is the plan.
5...d6 — supports e5 and opens the c8-bishop's diagonal. Solid as concrete.
6.c3 — prep a future d4 and give the bishop a c2 retreat. Tiny move, big plans.
6...a6 — stops Bb5/Nb5 ideas and prepares to keep the bishop. Prophylaxis: stopping their fun before it starts.
7.a4 — grab queenside space and stop Black's …b5. A little land grab.
7...Ba7 — tuck the bishop in the corner, safe but still aimed at the centre.
8.Re1 — rook to e1, backing e4 and lining up the e-file. Quietly useful.
8...O-O — Black castles. Everyone's safe; the real chess starts.
9.Nbd2 — the famous Italian knight tour begins: heading for f1–g3 (or c4). Slow but deadly.
9...Be6 — Black offers to trade off your good bishop and finishes developing.
10.Bxe6 — accept the trade; it hands Black doubled e-pawns. A long-term structural plus for you.
10...fxe6 — Black must recapture this way, accepting the doubled pawns in return for a half-open f-file.
11.b4 — start expanding on the queenside, gaining space and eyeing b5/c4 breaks. This is your side of the board.
11...Qe7 — Black connects the rooks and prepares to use that f-file.
12.Qb3 — pile onto the queenside and hit the weak e6-pawn. You're slowly turning the screws — exactly the Pianissimo dream. Welcome to a long, pleasant squeeze.
v.plan: This is a slow manoeuvring game and you hold the long-term trumps: Black has doubled e-pawns (e5 and e6) which are permanent weaknesses. Your plan: expand on the queenside with b4–b5, manoeuvre that d2-knight to a great square (f1–g3 hitting f5, or c4 hitting d6/e5), and pile pressure on the weak e6/d6 pawns. Don't open the position carelessly — keep it controlled, improve your worst piece each move, and grind Black down. Black's counterplay is the f-file, so keep f2 defended. Patience wins this.

notes: 1.e4 — centre, freedom, the usual.
1...e5 — classical reply.
2.Nf3 — develop, hit e5.
2...Nc6 — defend, develop.
3.Bc4 — bishop locks onto f7.
3...Bc5 — mirror. Both sides loaded.
4.b4!? — THE Evans Gambit. Chuck a pawn at the bishop like 'catch!' The point: lure the bishop away, then grab the centre with tempo. Pure 1800s romance.
4...Bxb4 — Black accepts the gift. Free pawn! (the bill comes later.)
5.c3 — kick the bishop again and prep d4. Buying time with threats — exactly what a gambit needs.
5...Ba5 — the bishop keeps the pressure and stays active. The most flexible retreat.
6.d4 — there it is. Blast the centre open while ahead in development. The pawn was just the cover charge.
6...exd4 — Black grabs again, but the development clock is ticking.
7.O-O — castle and open the floodgates; your rooks and bishops are itching.
7...d6 — Black throws up a wall and gives the king some air. Survival mode.
8.cxd4 — recapture, and now you have a monster centre AND a big development lead for one pawn. A bargain.
8...Bb6 — the bishop drops to a safe diagonal, eyeing your centre.
9.Nc3 — develop with tempo, eyeing d5 and e4. Everyone's coming to the party.
9...Bg4 — Black pins your f3-knight to add pressure on d4 and slow you down.
10.Bb5 — a clever pin-breaker: you pin the c6-knight right back and threaten ideas against Black's king.
10...Kf8 — ugh, Black has to step the king aside (can't castle now). A small triumph for your initiative.
11.Be3 — develop the last bishop, defend d4, and complete your beautiful setup. Every piece is out.
11...Nge7 — Black scrambles to develop and connect. You have a huge, classic Evans Gambit position: full development, big centre, attack brewing — all for a single pawn.
v.plan: Classic Evans Gambit payoff: you've traded a pawn for a massive lead in development, a big d4+e4 centre, and Black's king stuck on f8 unable to castle. Now ATTACK. Plans: play d5 to open lines and rip the centre, swing a rook to the e- or c-file, and target Black's stranded king. Moves like Qb3/Qd2, Rad1, and a timely d5 or e5 break are your bread and butter. Speed matters — your edge is development, so strike before Black untangles and consolidates. If Black ever manages to castle-by-hand and trade pieces, your pawn deficit starts to matter, so keep the pressure relentless.

notes: 1.e4 — centre grab.
1...e5 — bold central reply.
2.Nf3 — develop, threaten e5.
2...Nc6 — defend e5.
3.Bc4 — bishop targets f7. Remember that square — it's about to get famous.
3...Nf6 — the Two Knights. Black plays for activity, not safety.
4.Ng5!? — the cheeky knight lunges at f7. Snobs call it a beginner move; the people who've studied it call it a winning attack. It double-hits f7.
4...d5 — Black's only good reply: block the bishop and hit back in the centre.
5.exd5 — grab the pawn and keep the f7 pressure alive.
5...Nxd5?! — the natural recapture, walking into the Fried Liver. (The safe 5...Na5 exists, but where's the fun?)
6.Nxf7!! — the SACRIFICE. The knight smashes f7, giving up a piece to drag the king into the open and hunt it. Frying beginners since the 1600s.
6...Kxf7 — Black almost has to take. The king now stands in the middle of the board in his pyjamas.
7.Qf3+ — check, and it double-attacks the d5-knight. You're winning the piece back with interest.
7...Ke6 — the king must step UP to defend d5. Yes, the king on e6 on move 7. Terrifying but forced.
8.Nc3 — pile another attacker on the pinned d5-knight, developing with menace.
8...Nb4 — Black counterattacks your queen and eyes c2. Active defence — the critical try.
9.Qe4 — keep the d5-knight pinned, defend, and stay aimed at the centre. Cool under fire.
9...c6 — Black shores up the d5-knight with a pawn. Building a fortress around the exposed king.
10.a3 — kick the b4-knight back before it gets ideas about c2.
10...Na6 — the knight retreats to the rim; Black is tied in knots but materially up a piece.
11.d4 — open the centre and bring your last pieces toward the naked king. The bishop on c1 and rooks join in.
11...Nac7 — Black reroutes to defend d5 and e6. White has a ferocious attack and full practical compensation — in real games, defending this with your king on e6 is a nightmare. Hunt the king.
v.plan: You sacrificed a knight but Black's king is stuck in the centre on e6 and can never feel safe — that's your whole compensation, so you must ATTACK and not let Black consolidate. Plans: open lines toward the king with d4–d5 breaks, develop every piece with tempo (Bc1, O-O-O, rooks to the centre/e-file), and keep the d5-knight pinned and pressured. Castle queenside fast and throw the whole army at e6. Practically, Black has to find a long series of only-moves to survive, so keep checking, keep threatening, and don't trade queens — the attack is everything. If the king ever escapes to safety and Black untangles, you're down material, so make every move a threat.

notes: 1.e4 — open the centre.
1...e5 — classical.
2.Nf3 — develop, hit e5.
2...Nc6 — defend.
3.Bc4 — the f7 stare.
3...Nf6 — Two Knights, eyeing e4.
4.Ng5 — White lunges at f7 expecting 4...d5. But Black has a wild surprise…
4...Bc5!? — the TRAXLER. Black ignores the threat to f7 entirely and aims at f2. 'You attack my f7? I'll attack your f2 — and I won't blink first.' Madness, and almost sound.
5.Nxf7 — White takes the bait, forking queen and rook. Looks crushing… watch.
5...Bxf2+!! — Black answers with their OWN sacrifice on f2. Two sacs, two cold kings incoming. The most fun you can have in an opening.
6.Kxf2 — the king grabs the bishop (the critical, greedy try).
6...Nxe4+ — check! Black's pieces flood in with tempo while White's king walks the plank.
7.Kg1 — the king scuttles toward the corner, praying for cover.
7...Qh4 — bring the queen in, threatening nasty stuff on f2 and h2. Black has thrown a bishop at the king and is not sorry.
8.g3 — White tries to block the queen and build a wall.
8...Nxg3! — nope. Black blasts the wall with another sac. Relentless.
9.hxg3 — White takes the knight (basically forced).
9...Qxg3+ — the queen crashes in with check. The attack rolls on.
10.Kf1 — the king dodges to f1, still very nervous.
10...Rf8 — Black brings the LAST piece into the attack, pinning down the f7-knight and opening lines. Every Black piece is now screaming at the king.
11.Qh5 — White desperately tries to trade queens and survive, offering some relief.

11...d5! — Black blasts the centre open to bring the c8-bishop into the assault and refuses to let White breathe. Black has a raging attack and huge practical chances for the sacrificed material. The Traxler: where 'objectively unclear' meets 'absurdly fun.'
v.plan: You (as Black) have sacrificed material for a monster attack on White's exposed king — so your entire job is to keep the initiative and never let White untangle or trade into safety. Plans: open more lines with …d5 and …Bg4/…Bf5 to drag the last pieces in, keep the queen active around g3/h2/f2, and bring the rook on f8 and the c8-bishop into the hunt. Avoid trading queens unless it wins material — the attack is your compensation. If White consolidates and trades down, you're worse, so play fast, forcing, and fearless. Calculate the checks and keep White's king on the run.

notes: 1.e4 — centre, go.
1...e5 — classical reply.
2.Nf3 — develop, threaten e5.
2...Nc6 — defend.
3.Bc4 — bishop takes aim at f7.
3...Bc5 — Black mirrors.
4.d4!? — White cracks the centre open immediately, gambit-style. Welcome to the Max Lange zone.
4...exd4 — Black takes the pawn.
5.O-O — castle and pour gasoline on the position. You want open lines, fast.
5...Nf6 — Black develops and grabs at e4.
6.e5! — the thematic thrust, kicking the f6-knight and seizing space. Razor-sharp now.
6...d5 — Black hits back, blocking the bishop and trying to untangle.
7.exf6 — grab the knight; the f6-pawn becomes a thorn in Black's position.
7...dxc4 — Black grabs the bishop back. Material's level, the position's on fire.
8.Re1+ — check! The rook swings to the open e-file with tempo. Every move comes with a threat.
8...Be6 — Black blocks with the bishop, the only sensible square.
9.Ng5 — pile onto the pinned e6-bishop. Pieces swarming.
9...Qd5 — Black centralises the queen to defend e6 and hold things together. Gutsy.
10.Nc3 — develop with tempo, hit the queen, add an attacker. The whole army's in.
10...Qf5 — the queen sidesteps and keeps defending e6.
11.Nce4 — reroute the knight to e4, a dream square hitting d6/f6/g5 and supporting the attack. Black is getting squeezed.
11...Bf8 — Black has to grovel: the bishop drops back to defend g7 and the king. Passive but necessary.
12.Nxe6 — White cashes in, smashing the e6-bishop and wrecking Black's structure around the king.
12...fxe6 — Black recaptures, but now has shattered pawns (e6, e6-ish mess) and a draughty king. White has a powerful, lasting attack and the better structure. The Max Lange delivers.
v.plan: You've broken open Black's kingside and saddled them with a wrecked pawn structure and an exposed king — now press the attack and target those weaknesses. Plans: bring your queen and rooks to the e- and d-files to hammer the loose e6-pawn and the king, keep the strong knight on e4 (it's a beast), and look for the f6-pawn (if still there) as a battering ram. Don't let Black trade queens and consolidate — keep pieces on for the attack. Convert by either mating the stuck king or winning the weak pawns and heading to a better endgame. Precision matters: the Max Lange is sharp for both sides, so calculate carefully before committing.

notes: 1.e4 — open the centre.
1...e5 — classical.
2.Nf3 — develop, hit e5.
2...Nc6 — defend.
3.Bc4 — the f7 sniper sets up.
3...Be7 — the Hungarian Defense. Instead of the spicy 3...Bc5 or 3...Nf6, Black just plops the bishop on e7. Modest, solid, drama-free. 'No thanks to your sharp lines,' says Black.
4.d4 — White happily takes the big centre, since Black played it safe.
4...exd4 — Black trades to avoid getting squashed.
5.Nxd4 — recapture with the knight, sitting pretty in the centre.
5...Nf6 — develop and poke e4. A tidy, compact setup.
6.Nc3 — develop, defend e4, eye d5. Healthy.
6...O-O — Black tucks the king away. Safety first.
7.O-O — White castles too. Both kings cozy.
7...d6 — Black props up the centre and frees the c8-bishop. Small but solid.
8.h3 — a useful luft move, stopping any …Bg4 pin before it annoys you.
8...Re8 — rook to the e-file, eyeing e4.
9.Re1 — match it: rook to e1, reinforcing e4 and the e-file. Build-up phase.
9...Bf8 — Black re-routes the bishop to its best diagonal (toward g7) for flexible defence.
10.Bf4 — develop with pressure on d6, a slightly soft spot in Black's camp.
10...Nxd4 — Black trades a pair of knights to ease the slightly cramped position.
11.Qxd4 — recapture with the queen, beautifully centralised. White has more space and a pleasant, risk-free edge; Black is solid but passive. A calm, strategic battle lies ahead.
v.plan: You have a small but safe space advantage with no weaknesses — this is a 'nurse the edge' position, not a knockout. Plans: use your extra central space to manoeuvre pieces to good squares, keep an eye on Black's slightly weak d6-pawn, and consider expanding with moves like Rad1, Bg3 (pressuring d6), and maybe a later e5 or Nd5 break when well-prepared. Don't overpress — Black's position is solid, so improve slowly and keep control. The plan is to slowly increase pressure and provoke a weakness; if Black sits passively, you can gain space on either wing. Trade into a better endgame if the chance appears.

notes: 1.e4 — centre, freedom.
1...e5 — classical reply.
2.Nf3 — develop and threaten e5.
2...Nc6 — defend.
3.d4!? — the Scotch move order. Crack the centre open on move 3, before even developing the bishop. Aggressive intent, declared early.
3...exd4 — Black takes the pawn.
4.Bc4 — NOW the bishop comes out — Scotch Gambit. You offer the d4-pawn for fast development and an attack on f7.
4...Bc5 — Black develops actively and aims at f2. No playing scared.
5.c3 — offer ANOTHER pawn to blast the centre open and gain time. Gambiteers gonna gambit.
5...dxc3 — Black grabs it (declining is fine too, but free pawns tempt).
6.Nxc3 — recapture, fully developed and ahead in the development race. Two pieces out and a target on f7.
6...d6 — Black builds a shell and opens the light bishop's diagonal.
7.Qb3 — double-attack: the queen joins the bishop glaring at f7. Two attackers on the weak spot — alarm bells.
7...Qd7 — Black defends f7 with the queen, the only tidy way to hold.
8.Ng5 — pile a THIRD attacker on f7. You're going all-in on the classic target.
8...Ne5 — Black blocks the bishop's diagonal with the knight, defending f7 and offering to grab the bishop pair.
9.Bb5 — keep the pin alive and dodge the trade, harassing Black's queen and c6.
9...c6 — Black kicks the bishop and shores up d5/b5.
10.f4! — a strong thrust: kick the e5-knight and open the f-file toward Black's king. The initiative rolls on.
10...Bxg1 — Black grabs the rook in the corner (a desperado), accepting messy complications.
11.Rxg1 — recapture. You've given the exchange but have a raging initiative, open lines, and Black's king stuck in the centre. Full-blooded gambit chaos with you calling the shots.
v.plan: You're down a little material but you have a screaming initiative and Black's king is stuck in the centre — so attack while Black is tangled up. Plans: open lines toward the king with f4–f5 and e-file pressure, keep the queen and bishop aimed at f7/the light squares, and bring the g1-rook into the game fast. Castle queenside if you get the chance to connect rooks and add a third attacker. The key is speed and forcing moves — every move should be a threat so Black never gets to develop and consolidate. If Black manages to trade pieces and untangle the king to safety, the material will start to matter, so don't relent. Calculate the sacrifices; this line rewards bold, accurate attacking play.

3.Bc4 — bishop targets f7. Remember that square — it's about to get famous.
3...Nf6 — the Two Knights. Black plays for activity, not safety.
4.Ng5!? — the cheeky knight lunges at f7. Snobs call it a beginner move; the people who've studied it call it a winning attack. It double-hits f7.
4...d5 — Black's only good reply: block the bishop and hit back in the centre.
5.exd5 — grab the pawn and keep the f7 pressure alive.
5...Nxd5?! — the natural recapture, walking into the Fried Liver. (The safe 5...Na5 exists, but where's the fun?)
6.Nxf7!! — the SACRIFICE. The knight smashes f7, giving up a piece to drag the king into the open and hunt it. Frying beginners since the 1600s.
6...Kxf7 — Black almost has to take. The king now stands in the middle of the board in his pyjamas.
7.Qf3+ — check, and it double-attacks the d5-knight. You're winning the piece back with interest.
7...Ke6 — the king must step UP to defend d5. Yes, the king on e6 on move 7. Terrifying but forced.
8.Nc3 — pile another attacker on the pinned d5-knight, developing with menace.
8...Nb4 — Black counterattacks your queen and eyes c2. Active defence — the critical try.
9.Qe4 — keep the d5-knight pinned, defend, and stay aimed at the centre. Cool under fire.
9...c6 — Black shores up the d5-knight with a pawn. Building a fortress around the exposed king.
10.a3 — kick the b4-knight back before it gets ideas about c2.
10...Na6 — the knight retreats to the rim; Black is tied in knots but materially up a piece.
11.d4 — open the centre and bring your last pieces toward the naked king. The bishop on c1 and rooks join in.
11...Nac7 — Black reroutes to defend d5 and e6. White has a ferocious attack and full practical compensation — in real games, defending this with your king on e6 is a nightmare. Hunt the king.
variations.plan: You sacrificed a knight but Black's king is stuck in the centre on e6 and can never feel safe — that's your whole compensation, so you must ATTACK and not let Black consolidate. Plans: open lines toward the king with d4–d5 breaks, develop every piece with tempo (Bc1, O-O-O, rooks to the centre/e-file), and keep the d5-knight pinned and pressured. Castle queenside fast and throw the whole army at e6. Practically, Black has to find a long series of only-moves to survive, so keep checking, keep threatening, and don't trade queens — the attack is everything. If the king ever escapes to safety and Black untangles, you're down material, so make every move a threat.

notes: 1.e4 — open the centre.
1...e5 — classical.
2.Nf3 — develop, hit e5.
2...Nc6 — defend.
3.Bc4 — the f7 stare.
3...Nf6 — Two Knights, eyeing e4.
4.Ng5 — White lunges at f7 expecting 4...d5. But Black has a wild surprise…
4...Bc5!? — the TRAXLER. Black ignores the threat to f7 entirely and aims at f2. 'You attack my f7? I'll attack your f2 — and I won't blink first.' Madness, and almost sound.
5.Nxf7 — White takes the bait, forking queen and rook. Looks crushing… watch.
5...Bxf2+!! — Black answers with their OWN sacrifice on f2. Two sacs, two cold kings incoming. The most fun you can have in an opening.
6.Kxf2 — the king grabs the bishop (the critical, greedy try).
6...Nxe4+ — check! Black's pieces flood in with tempo while White's king walks the plank.
7.Kg1 — the king scuttles toward the corner, praying for cover.
7...Qh4 — bring the queen in, threatening nasty stuff on f2 and h2. Black has thrown a bishop at the king and is not sorry.
8.g3 — White tries to block the queen and build a wall.
8...Nxg3! — nope. Black blasts the wall with another sac. Relentless.
9.hxg3 — White takes the knight (basically forced).
9...Qxg3+ — the queen crashes in with check. The attack rolls on.
10.Kf1 — the king dodges to f1, still very nervous.
10...Rf8 — Black brings the LAST piece into the attack, pinning down the f7-knight and opening lines. Every Black piece is now screaming at the king.
11.Qh5 — White desperately tries to trade queens and survive, offering some relief.

11...d5! — Black blasts the centre open to bring the c8-bishop into the assault and refuses to let White breathe. Black has a raging attack and huge practical chances for the sacrificed material. The Traxler: where 'objectively unclear' meets 'absurdly fun.'
variations.plan: You (as Black) have sacrificed material for a monster attack on White's exposed king — so your entire job is to keep the initiative and never let White untangle or trade into safety. Plans: open more lines with …d5 and …Bg4/…Bf5 to drag the last pieces in, keep the queen active around g3/h2/f2, and bring the rook on f8 and the c8-bishop into the hunt. Avoid trading queens unless it wins material — the attack is your compensation. If White consolidates and trades down, you're worse, so play fast, forcing, and fearless. Calculate the checks and keep White's king on the run.

notes: 1.e4 — centre, go.
1...e5 — classical reply.
2.Nf3 — develop, threaten e5.
2...Nc6 — defend.
3.Bc4 — bishop takes aim at f7.
3...Bc5 — Black mirrors.
4.d4!? — White cracks the centre open immediately, gambit-style. Welcome to the Max Lange zone.
4...exd4 — Black takes the pawn.
5.O-O — castle and pour gasoline on the position. You want open lines, fast.
5...Nf6 — Black develops and grabs at e4.
6.e5! — the thematic thrust, kicking the f6-knight and seizing space. Razor-sharp now.
6...d5 — Black hits back, blocking the bishop and trying to untangle.
7.exf6 — grab the knight; the f6-pawn becomes a thorn in Black's position.
7...dxc4 — Black grabs the bishop back. Material's level, the position's on fire.
8.Re1+ — check! The rook swings to the open e-file with tempo. Every move comes with a threat.
8...Be6 — Black blocks with the bishop, the only sensible square.
9.Ng5 — pile onto the pinned e6-bishop. Pieces swarming.
9...Qd5 — Black centralises the queen to defend e6 and hold things together. Gutsy.
10.Nc3 — develop with tempo, hit the queen, add an attacker. The whole army's in.
10...Qf5 — the queen sidesteps and keeps defending e6.
11.Nce4 — reroute the knight to e4, a dream square hitting d6/f6/g5 and supporting the attack. Black is getting squeezed.
11...Bf8 — Black has to grovel: the bishop drops back to defend g7 and the king. Passive but necessary.
12.Nxe6 — White cashes in, smashing the e6-bishop and wrecking Black's structure around the king.
12...fxe6 — Black recaptures, but now has shattered pawns (e6, e6-ish mess) and a draughty king. White has a powerful, lasting attack and the better structure. The Max Lange delivers.
variations.plan: You've broken open Black's kingside and saddled them with a wrecked pawn structure and an exposed king — now press the attack and target those weaknesses. Plans: bring your queen and rooks to the e- and d-files to hammer the loose e6-pawn and the king, keep the strong knight on e4 (it's a beast), and look for the f6-pawn (if still there) as a battering ram. Don't let Black trade queens and consolidate — keep pieces on for the attack. Convert by either mating the stuck king or winning the weak pawns and heading to a better endgame. Precision matters: the Max Lange is sharp for both sides, so calculate carefully before committing.

notes: 1.e4 — open the centre.
1...e5 — classical.
2.Nf3 — develop, hit e5.
2...Nc6 — defend.
3.Bc4 — the f7 sniper sets up.
3...Be7 — the Hungarian Defense. Instead of the spicy 3...Bc5 or 3...Nf6, Black just plops the bishop on e7. Modest, solid, drama-free. 'No thanks to your sharp lines,' says Black.
4.d4 — White happily takes the big centre, since Black played it safe.
4...exd4 — Black trades to avoid getting squashed.
5.Nxd4 — recapture with the knight, sitting pretty in the centre.
5...Nf6 — develop and poke e4. A tidy, compact setup.
6.Nc3 — develop, defend e4, eye d5. Healthy.
6...O-O — Black tucks the king away. Safety first.
7.O-O — White castles too. Both kings cozy.
7...d6 — Black props up the centre and frees the c8-bishop. Small but solid.
8.h3 — a useful luft move, stopping any …Bg4 pin before it annoys you.
8...Re8 — rook to the e-file, eyeing e4.
9.Re1 — match it: rook to e1, reinforcing e4 and the e-file. Build-up phase.
9...Bf8 — Black re-routes the bishop to its best diagonal (toward g7) for flexible defence.
10.Bf4 — develop with pressure on d6, a slightly soft spot in Black's camp.
10...Nxd4 — Black trades a pair of knights to ease the slightly cramped position.
11.Qxd4 — recapture with the queen, beautifully centralised. White has more space and a pleasant, risk-free edge; Black is solid but passive. A calm, strategic battle lies ahead.
variations.plan: You have a small but safe space advantage with no weaknesses — this is a 'nurse the edge' position, not a knockout. Plans: use your extra central space to manoeuvre pieces to good squares, keep an eye on Black's slightly weak d6-pawn, and consider expanding with moves like Rad1, Bg3 (pressuring d6), and maybe a later e5 or Nd5 break when well-prepared. Don't overpress — Black's position is solid, so improve slowly and keep control. The plan is to slowly increase pressure and provoke a weakness; if Black sits passively, you can gain space on either wing. Trade into a better endgame if the chance appears.

notes: 1.e4 — centre, freedom.
1...e5 — classical reply.
2.Nf3 — develop and threaten e5.
2...Nc6 — defend.
3.d4!? — the Scotch move order. Crack the centre open on move 3, before even developing the bishop. Aggressive intent, declared early.
3...exd4 — Black takes the pawn.
4.Bc4 — NOW the bishop comes out — Scotch Gambit. You offer the d4-pawn for fast development and an attack on f7.
4...Bc5 — Black develops actively and aims at f2. No playing scared.
5.c3 — offer ANOTHER pawn to blast the centre open and gain time. Gambiteers gonna gambit.
5...dxc3 — Black grabs it (declining is fine too, but free pawns tempt).
6.Nxc3 — recapture, fully developed and ahead in the development race. Two pieces out and a target on f7.
6...d6 — Black builds a shell and opens the light bishop's diagonal.
7.Qb3 — double-attack: the queen joins the bishop glaring at f7. Two attackers on the weak spot — alarm bells.
7...Qd7 — Black defends f7 with the queen, the only tidy way to hold.
8.Ng5 — pile a THIRD attacker on f7. You're going all-in on the classic target.
8...Ne5 — Black blocks the bishop's diagonal with the knight, defending f7 and offering to grab the bishop pair.
9.Bb5 — keep the pin alive and dodge the trade, harassing Black's queen and c6.
9...c6 — Black kicks the bishop and shores up d5/b5.
10.f4! — a strong thrust: kick the e5-knight and open the f-file toward Black's king. The initiative rolls on.
10...Bxg1 — Black grabs the rook in the corner (a desperado), accepting messy complications.
11.Rxg1 — recapture. You've given the exchange but have a raging initiative, open lines, and Black's king stuck in the centre. Full-blooded gambit chaos with you calling the shots.
variations.plan: You're down a little material but you have a screaming initiative and Black's king is stuck in the centre — so attack while Black is tangled up. Plans: open lines toward the king with f4–f5 and e-file pressure, keep the queen and bishop aimed at f7/the light squares, and bring the g1-rook into the game fast. Castle queenside if you get the chance to connect rooks and add a third attacker. The key is speed and forcing moves — every move should be a threat so Black never gets to develop and consolidate. If Black manages to trade pieces and untangle the king to safety, the material will start to matter, so don't relent. Calculate the sacrifices; this line rewards bold, accurate attacking play.

intro.summary: The Italian Game is the most welcoming of the great open games — and secretly one of the deepest. After 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4, the bishop takes dead aim at f7, the one square only the enemy king defends. You get fast development, open lines, and a clear plan — with your pick of personality: squeeze slowly with the quiet d3 lines, or tear the position open with the Evans Gambit, the Fried Liver, and the Max Lange. It's the perfect first serious opening: easy to start, rich enough to play for a lifetime.
plans: Keep the light-squared bishop pointed at f7 — that diagonal is your permanent source of pressure.
Pick your centre: c3 then d4 for a big pawn duo, or the calm d3 for a slow, solid build-up.
Castle early and connect the rooks before you commit to attacking the king or grinding an edge.
Learn the sharp lines cold — Fried Liver, Evans Gambit, Traxler — one f7 tactic can end the game by move ten.
In the quiet lines, save the d4 break for the right moment to open the position for your better pieces.

openings.desc: The friendliest of the great open games — and secretly one of the deepest. 3.Bc4 aims straight at f7, the one square only the king defends, with a choice of quiet positional squeezes or wild gambits: the Evans, the Fried Liver, the Max Lange.

notes: 1.e4 — stake a claim in the centre and free the bishop and queen. The most-played move in chess.
1...e5 — Black grabs an equal share of the centre. The classical open game begins.
2.Nf3 — develop the knight and hit e5 at the same time. Pressure from move two.
2...Nc6 — defend e5 and develop. The natural, best reply.
3.Bb5 — the Ruy López. Instead of aiming at f7, White pins the knight that guards e5 — a slow, deep squeeze rather than a quick jab.
3...a6 — the Morphy move. Ask the bishop its intentions before doing anything else.
4.Ba4 — keep the bishop on its long diagonal; it stays a thorn for the whole game.
4...Nf6 — develop and hit the e4-pawn. Black plays actively.
5.O-O — castle first. The e4-pawn looks free but grabbing it is dangerous for Black.
5...Be7 — quiet, solid development, ready to castle.
6.Re1 — re-defend e4 and put the rook where it belongs.
6...b5 — kick the bishop before it settles in.
7.Bb3 — back to the ideal diagonal, eyeing f7 and d5.
7...d6 — shore up e5 and free the light-squared bishop.
8.c3 — the key Spanish move: prepare d4 and give the bishop a retreat square on c2.
8...O-O — Black is fully developed and safe.
9.h3 — a small but vital pause: stop ...Bg4 pinning the knight before you push d4.
9...Na5 — the Chigorin plan: the knight heads over to trade the strong b3-bishop.
10.Bc2 — sidestep and keep the bishop; it now aims at h7 for a future kingside attack.
10...c5 — Black grabs queenside space and prepares to challenge the centre.
11.d4 — the big central break at last, handing White a lasting space edge.
11...Qc7 — Black supports the centre and reaches the main tabiya. You have more space, the Bc2 aimed at Black's king, and a rich manoeuvring game to squeeze.
v.plan: You've reached the great Closed Ruy tabiya with a space advantage and the classic Bc2 + Qd3 battery aiming at h7. Don't release the central tension too soon — keep Black guessing. Manoeuvre your knight Nbd2–f1–g3 toward the kingside, complete the battery with Qd3, and build a slow attack against Black's king while your extra space lets you improve every piece. This is chess as a long, patient squeeze.

notes: 1.e4 — stake a claim in the centre and free the bishop and queen. The most-played move in chess.
1...e5 — Black grabs an equal share of the centre. The classical open game begins.
2.Nf3 — develop the knight and hit e5 at the same time. Pressure from move two.
2...Nc6 — defend e5 and develop. The natural, best reply.
3.Bb5 — the Ruy López. Instead of aiming at f7, White pins the knight that guards e5 — a slow, deep squeeze rather than a quick jab.
3...Nf6 — the Berlin. Black ignores the pin and counter-attacks e4 — Kramnik's rock that stopped Kasparov.
4.O-O — castle and dare Black to grab the e4-pawn.
4...Nxe4 — Black accepts; now the deep Berlin theory begins.
5.d4 — strike the centre and open lines against the e4-knight.
5...Nd6 — the knight retreats, hitting the b5-bishop and blunting White's initiative.
6.Bxc6 — trade before you're kicked, damaging Black's pawns.
6...dxc6 — recapture toward the centre, opening queen and bishop.
7.dxe5 — win the pawn back and hit the d6-knight.
7...Nf5 — reroute the knight to a fine square.
8.Qxd8+ — force the famous queen trade; Black loses the right to castle.
8...Kxd8 — the Berlin endgame. No queens, but Black's king is stuck in the middle.
9.Nc3 — develop and start restricting Black's pieces.
9...Ke8 — the king walks toward safety by hand.
10.h3 — a handy little move, keeping g4 in reserve and stopping ...Bg4 ideas.
10...h5 — Black claims kingside space to give his pieces squares.
11.Bf4 — develop with tempo, gripping the dark squares.
11...Be7 — Black finishes developing. You hold the Berlin edge: better structure, the safer king, and a risk-free grind.
v.plan: This is the famous Berlin endgame — queens off, but you hold the better pawn structure and safer king. Play for a small, permanent edge: activate your rooks, target Black's doubled c-pawns, and improve your pieces slowly. You can press for a very long time without ever standing worse, which is exactly why the Berlin is trusted at the very top. If you'd rather keep queens on, 4.d3 (the Anti-Berlin) sidesteps all of this.

notes: 1.e4 — stake a claim in the centre and free the bishop and queen. The most-played move in chess.
1...e5 — Black grabs an equal share of the centre. The classical open game begins.
2.Nf3 — develop the knight and hit e5 at the same time. Pressure from move two.
2...Nc6 — defend e5 and develop. The natural, best reply.
3.Bb5 — the Ruy López. Instead of aiming at f7, White pins the knight that guards e5 — a slow, deep squeeze rather than a quick jab.
3...a6 — question the bishop.
4.Bxc6 — the Exchange Variation. Give up the bishop to wreck Black's queenside pawns.
4...dxc6 — recapture toward the centre, keeping the pawns connected.
5.O-O — castle. You're playing for structure, not a quick attack.
5...f6 — Black props up e5; his doubled c-pawns are balanced by the two bishops.
6.d4 — challenge the centre at once, before Black consolidates.
6...exd4 — Black takes; keeping the tension would favour you.
7.Nxd4 — recapture with a nicely centralised knight.
7...c5 — kick the knight and use the bishop pair to grab space.
8.Nb3 — retreat, keeping an eye on c5 and a5.
8...Qxd1 — Black steers into a safe endgame with the queen trade.
9.Rxd1 — recapture; the queens are gone and the real battle is structural.

9...Bd7 — Black develops and connects. You've reached the classic Exchange endgame: your healthy 4-vs-3 kingside majority can make a passed pawn — Black's doubled c-pawns cannot. That's the trump you play for.
v.plan: The Exchange Ruy is a pure pawn-structure battle. You gave up the bishop pair to saddle Black with doubled c-pawns. Your trump: a healthy 4-vs-3 kingside majority that can create a passed pawn, while Black's crippled queenside majority can't. Head for the endgame, keep it simple, march your kingside pawns, and let the better structure decide. It's the textbook 'good structure beats bishop pair' lesson.

2...Nc6 — defend e5 and develop. The natural, best reply.

3...a6 — the Morphy move.

4...Nf6 — develop and hit e4.
5.O-O — castle.
5...Be7 — heading for the Closed Ruy.

6...b5 — kick the bishop.
7.Bb3 — the ideal diagonal.
7...O-O — Black castles, delaying ...d6 with a deep idea in mind.
8.c3 — prepare d4 as usual. But now...
8...d5!? — the Marshall Attack! Black sacrifices a pawn for a raging kingside initiative — one of the most feared gambits in chess.
9.exd5 — accept the challenge; declining defeats the whole point of the gambit.
9...Nxd5 — the knight recaptures, ready to swing to the kingside.
10.Nxe5 — grab the second pawn. You must now defend with precision.
10...Nxe5 — Black removes a key defender.

11...c6 — the modern main move, keeping the d5-knight supported and preparing ...Bd6 and ...Qh4 with a fierce attack. You're up material but must know the theory and return a pawn at the right moment to reach a safe, better endgame.
v.plan: You're facing the Marshall Attack — Black has sacrificed a pawn for a lasting kingside initiative. Your job is defence and precision: know the main-line moves, don't get greedy, and be ready to give a pawn back to kill the attack and reach a slightly better endgame. Survive the storm and your material tells. If defending sharp positions isn't your style, an Anti-Marshall with 8.h3 or 8.a4 sidesteps the whole thing.

notes: 1.e4 — stake a claim in the centre and free the bishop and queen. The most-played move in chess.
1...e5 — Black grabs an equal share of the centre. The classical open game begins.
2.Nf3 — develop the knight and hit e5 at the same time. Pressure from move two.
2...Nc6 — defend e5 and develop. The natural, best reply.
3.Bb5 — the Ruy López. Instead of aiming at f7, White pins the knight that guards e5 — a slow, deep squeeze rather than a quick jab.
3...a6 — question the bishop.
4.Ba4 — keep it on the diagonal.
4...Nf6 — develop and hit e4.
5.O-O — castle and offer the e4-pawn.
5...Nxe4 — the Open Spanish: Black grabs the pawn for active piece play.
6.d4 — strike the centre; you'll win the pawn back with pressure.
6...b5 — gain time on the bishop before it's too late.
7.Bb3 — retreat to the a2-g8 diagonal.
7...d5 — the key move: Black supports the e4-knight with a pawn and seizes the centre.
8.dxe5 — take on e5; the position opens into sharp piece play.
8...Be6 — develop and reinforce d5, the backbone of Black's centre.
9.c3 — solidify, give the bishop c2, and stop ...Nc3 tricks.

9...Be7 — Black completes development. You reach the main Open Ruy: a lively middlegame where you'll play Nbd2 and Bc2, pressure d5 and the e4-knight, and prove Black's active pieces are also a little loose.
v.plan: The Open Spanish is a lively, piece-heavy fight. Black's pieces are active (the e4-knight, Be6, Be7) but slightly loose. Your plan: manoeuvre Nbd2 to challenge the e4-knight, reroute the bishop to c2 aiming at h7, and press the d5-pawn. Play in the centre and on the kingside, target Black's airy structure, and remember the proud e4-knight can become a target. Precise piece play — not memorised tactics — wins here.

notes: 1.e4 — stake a claim in the centre and free the bishop and queen. The most-played move in chess.
1...e5 — Black grabs an equal share of the centre. The classical open game begins.
2.Nf3 — develop the knight and hit e5 at the same time. Pressure from move two.
2...Nc6 — defend e5 and develop. The natural, best reply.
3.Bb5 — the Ruy López. Instead of aiming at f7, White pins the knight that guards e5 — a slow, deep squeeze rather than a quick jab.
3...f5!? — the Schliemann. Black blasts the centre open with a wild gambit, ignoring development for chaos.
4.Nc3 — the calm, strong reply: develop and add a defender of e4 instead of grabbing material.
4...fxe4 — Black opens the f-file and hands over the pawn.
5.Nxe4 — recapture, centralising the knight on a great square.
5...d5 — kick the knight and open lines for Black's pieces — the point of the gambit.
6.Nxe5 — a strong in-between move: snatch e5 and hit the c6-knight before retreating.
6...dxe4 — Black takes the e4-knight, restoring some material.
7.Nxc6 — grab the knight; Black's structure is shattered.
7...Qg5 — Black lunges at g2 and e5, trying to justify the sacrifice with activity.
8.Qe2 — the cool defence: guard e4 and eye the pin down the e-file at Black's king.
8...Nf6 — Black develops and defends. White emerges a healthy pawn up with the safer position; accurate play refutes the gambit and leaves you clearly better.
v.plan: You've met the wild Schliemann with the solid 4.Nc3 and come out on top: an extra pawn, a better structure, and the safer king. Now consolidate — finish developing (d3/d4, Bf4 or Be3, castle), neutralise Black's activity down the f-file, and trade pieces toward a winning endgame. Black gambled on chaos; deny the chaos and your material edge decides the game.

openings.desc: The Spanish Opening — the deepest and most respected 1.e4 e5 system. 3.Bb5 pins the defender of e5 and begins a long strategic squeeze, from the marathon Closed Ruy to the rock-solid Berlin and the venomous Marshall.

intro.summary: The Ruy López — the Spanish Opening — is the deepest and most respected of all 1.e4 e5 openings, played at the highest level for over 150 years. With 3.Bb5, White pins the knight that defends e5 and begins a slow, strategic squeeze rather than an immediate assault. It leads to some of chess's richest battlegrounds: the marathon Closed Ruy, the rock-solid Berlin endgame, the venomous Marshall Attack, and the structural Exchange. If the Italian is where you learn to develop, the Ruy is where you learn to play chess.
plans: Pin and pressure: 3.Bb5 targets the defender of e5, then Ba4–Bb3 keeps the bishop on its long, dangerous diagonal.
Prepare the big centre with c3 and d4 — the Spanish break that opens the position once you're fully developed.
Reroute the bishop to c2 to build the classic Bc2 + Qd3 battery aimed at Black's h7.
Choose your weapon against sharp defences — accept the Marshall, or sidestep it with an Anti-Marshall (h3/a4).
In the Exchange and Berlin, forget attacking — play for a better structure and a risk-free endgame edge.
